questions.q: For the Hamiltonian H=(ħω/2)Z, what is the resulting time-evolution operator U(t)=exp(−iHt/ħ)?
options: The identity matrix at all times, since Z has no effect
diag(e^(−iωt/2), e^(+iωt/2)) -- a diagonal matrix, since Z itself is diagonal
A matrix that changes P(0) and P(1) over time for every input state
An off-diagonal matrix that swaps the |0⟩ and |1⟩ amplitudes
questions.explain: Because Z is diagonal with eigenvalues ±1, exponentiating −iHt/ħ gives a diagonal matrix with entries e^(∓iωt/2), verified to each have magnitude exactly 1 for any t.

questions.q: Applying U(t) at θ=ωt/2=π/4 to |0⟩ produces e^(−iπ/4)|0⟩. Why does this have zero observable effect?
options: Because e^(−iπ/4) equals exactly 1, so nothing actually changes mathematically
It's a global phase applied to the entire (single-component-populated) state, and since |0⟩ has nothing else to compare the phase against, probabilities are unchanged (P(0)=1, P(1)=0 still)
Because |0⟩ cannot be acted on by any unitary operator
Because global phases only apply to the |+⟩ state, never to |0⟩
questions.explain: e^(−iπ/4) has magnitude 1 (verified) but is not literally equal to 1 -- it's a genuine phase factor. Since it multiplies the entire (single-term) state, it's a global phase and therefore unobservable, unlike a phase appearing between two different components.

questions.q: Applying the same U(t) to |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 gives components (0.5−0.5i, 0.5+0.5i), with both probabilities still 0.5. What changed that IS physically observable?
options: A relative phase of e^(iπ/2)=i appeared between the |0⟩ and |1⟩ components, even though the individual measurement probabilities stayed the same
Nothing changed at all -- the result is physically identical to the original |+⟩
The |0⟩ and |1⟩ amplitudes swapped values entirely
The state's normalization was broken by the evolution
questions.explain: Factoring out the common phase e^(−iπ/4) from both components leaves a relative phase of e^(iπ/2)=i between them (verified) -- a real, physical change, even though |amplitude|² for each term is unchanged at 0.5.

questions.q: What does it mean for a matrix U to be 'unitary' (U†U=I), and why is this physically required for time evolution?
options: It means U preserves the inner product ⟨ψ|ψ⟩, guaranteeing that if a state starts normalized (total probability 1), it stays normalized at every later time
It is a purely mathematical convenience with no physical necessity
It means U can only be applied to the |0⟩ state, never to superpositions
It means U always leaves the state completely unchanged
questions.explain: U†U=I is exactly the condition that keeps ⟨ψ(t)|ψ(t)⟩ equal to 1 for all t -- total probability over all outcomes must always sum to 1, and unitarity is what guarantees evolution never breaks that.

questions.q: Why does the exact same operator U(t)=diag(e^(−iπ/4), e^(iπ/4)) produce an unobservable effect on |0⟩ but an observable one on |+⟩?
options: |0⟩ is not a valid input for a unitary operator, so no comparison is meaningful
The operator actually behaves differently depending on which state it's applied to
There is no real difference; both effects are equally observable

On |0⟩, the phase applies to the state's only nonzero component (a global phase, invisible); on |+⟩, the two components pick up different phases relative to each other, producing a physical relative phase that interference-based operations can detect
questions.explain: The same fixed diagonal matrix produces a global (unobservable) phase when only one component is populated, but a relative (observable) phase difference when two components are both populated, as with |+⟩ -- this is exactly the global-vs-relative-phase distinction made concrete.
